lead: IPv6 replaces the 32‑bit IPv4 address with a 128‑bit address. The larger space removes address shortage and allows automatic aggregation. A simplified header reduces processing load on routers. IPv6 is used on modern backbones, mobile networks and new campus links.
prereq: You need: basic IPv4 addressing from IPv4 addressing and the IPv4 header format from IPv4 datagram format.

blocks.text: An IPv6 address is 128 bits long. It is written as eight groups of four hexadecimal digits separated by colons. Example: 2001:0db8:85a3:0000:0000:8a2e:0370:7334.
Leading zeros in a group may be omitted. A group of all zeros may be replaced by a double colon ::, but only once in an address.

items: Split the address at each colon.
Remove leading zeros in each group.
Replace the longest run of consecutive zero groups by ::.

blocks.where: Addr is the full 128‑bit address; Prefix is the high‑order bits that identify the network; InterfaceID is the low‑order bits that identify the host.

items: Each group represents 16 bits.
A /64 prefix means the first 64 bits are the network part.
The remaining 64 bits form the Interface ID.

blocks.text: IPv6 defines three main unicast address types: global, link‑local, and unique‑local. Their scopes are global, link‑local, and local to a site (unique‑local) respectively. Global addresses are routable on the Internet. Link‑local addresses start with fe80:: and are used on a single link.
Multicast addresses begin with ff00:: and replace broadcast. Anycast addresses are assigned to multiple interfaces; the nearest one receives the packet.

items: Global unicast: 2000::/3.
Unique‑local: fc00::/7.
Link‑local: fe80::/10.

blocks.text: The hierarchical prefix allows ISPs to allocate large blocks to customers, which they can further subdivide without renumbering.
The IPv6 header is fixed at 40 bytes. It contains only the fields needed for basic forwarding.

items: Version (4 bits) = 6.
Traffic Class (8 bits) for QoS.
Flow Label (20 bits) for special handling.
Payload Length (16 bits) = size of the payload in octets, i.e., the number of bytes after the IPv6 header, including any extension headers and the upper‑layer data.
Next Header (8 bits) identifies the upper‑layer protocol.
Hop Limit (8 bits) decrements at each hop; packet is discarded at zero.
Source Address (128 bits).
Destination Address (128 bits).

blocks.text: There is no header checksum. Errors are detected by the upper‑layer protocol (TCP/UDP).
Transition mechanisms let IPv4‑only hosts communicate with IPv6‑only hosts during the migration period.

items: Dual‑stack: a device runs both IPv4 and IPv6 stacks.
Tunneling: IPv6 packets are encapsulated inside IPv4 packets (e.g., 6to4, Teredo).
NAT64/DNS64: IPv6‑only clients use a translator that maps IPv6 to IPv4 addresses.

blocks.text: ISPs often deploy NAT64 to let mobile phones using only IPv6 reach legacy IPv4 services such as an IRCTC booking site.

examples.question: An IPv6 address 2001:db8:acad:1::1/64 is assigned to a server. Identify the network prefix and interface ID. A packet with payload 1000 bytes is sent. What are the Version, Payload Length and Hop Limit values?
steps: Split the address into prefix (first 64 bits) and interface ID (last 64 bits).
Prefix = 2001:db8:acad:1::/64 because the first four groups form the network part.
Interface ID = ::1 because the remaining groups are all zeros except the last group 1.
Version field is always 6 for IPv6.
Payload Length field equals the size of the data after the header, here 1000 bytes.
Hop Limit defaults to 64 unless set otherwise.
examples.answer: Prefix = 2001:db8:acad:1::/64, Interface ID = ::1, Version = 6, Payload Length = 1000 bytes, Hop Limit = 64.
examples.check:
v = 6
payload = 1000
hop = 64
print(v)
print(payload)
print(hop)

traps: Treating the double colon :: as a single zero byte instead of a variable‑length zero run.
Assuming the Hop Limit is always 255; the default in most operating systems is 64.
Confusing the IPv6 Flow Label (20 bits) with the IPv4 Identification field used for fragmentation.
Using the IPv4 checksum value for IPv6 packets; IPv6 has no header checksum.

quiz.q: What is the size of an IPv6 address in bits?
Why can the double colon :: appear only once in an IPv6 address?
quiz.a: Because :: can replace any run of consecutive zero groups, it is allowed only once to avoid ambiguity. The convention is to use it for the longest run of zeros in the address.

quiz.q: Given the address 2001:0db8:85a3::8a2e:0370:7334/48, write the network prefix.
A router receives an IPv6 packet with Hop Limit = 1. What happens after the router processes the packet?
quiz.a: The router decrements Hop Limit to 0 and discards the packet, sending an ICMPv6 Time Exceeded message to the source.

quiz.q: Compare the IPv4 header checksum with the IPv6 design choice of removing it. What impact does this have on router processing?
quiz.a: Removing the checksum eliminates per‑hop checksum computation, speeding up forwarding. Error detection is shifted to upper‑layer protocols, which already perform checksums, so overall reliability is maintained.

beyond: Not for the exam. IPv6 address planning is a major topic in large data‑center deployments where hierarchical prefixes reduce routing table size. Research continues on IPv6 security extensions such as SEND and on optimizing NAT64 performance for IoT devices. New curricula add SDN‑based IPv6 automation and programmable header processing. To explore further, search for "IPv6 address autoconfiguration" and "Segment Routing over IPv6".
